questions.q: When two wave pulses overlap in a medium, the superposition principle states that the resultant disturbance is found how?
options: The amplitudes of the individual wave pulses add together to give the resultant wave, which is the sum of the individual waves
The faster wave continues and the slower wave is absorbed by the medium
The two waves swap frequencies and wavelengths at the point where they meet
The resultant amplitude is always the difference between the two individual amplitudes
questions.explanation: By superposition the resultant wave is the sum of the individual waves: the displacements of the medium add at every point, taking sign into account. After overlapping, the pulses pass through each other and continue on undisturbed.

questions.q: Two waves of the same frequency and amplitude interfere. Under what condition does complete destructive interference occur, cancelling to give zero resultant amplitude?
options: When the waves are in phase, with crests and troughs occurring simultaneously
When the waves have opposite phase, with one wave's peaks coinciding with the other wave's troughs
When the two waves travel in the same direction at different speeds
When one wave has twice the wavelength of the other
questions.explanation: Constructive interference occurs when waves are in phase and their amplitudes add to a larger value. Complete destructive interference occurs when two waves of the same frequency and amplitude have opposite phase, so one wave's peaks coincide with the other's troughs and they completely cancel.

questions.q: From memory, describe what happens when a wave on a string reflects from a fixed end versus a free end, and what stays the same about the reflected wave.
keyPoints: Reflection is the returning of a wave into the medium in which it was originally travelling when it strikes a barrier or the end of the medium.
When the end is fixed (unable to move), the reflected wave is inverted — this is called a change of phase.
When the end is free to move, the wave is reflected upright and unchanged, so there is no change of phase.
The reflected wave has the same speed, wavelength and frequency as the incident wave.
questions.explanation: The fixed-end inversion (change of phase) is the detail the syllabus rewards. If you also recalled that speed, wavelength and frequency are unchanged on reflection, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: In a standing wave, an incident wave coincides with a reflected wave that is opposite in phase to give evenly spaced nodes by destructive interference, and equal in phase to give antinodes by constructive interference. What is the wavelength of the waves involved in the standing wave, in terms of the distance between adjacent nodes?
options: The wavelength equals the distance between adjacent nodes
The wavelength of the waves involved in the standing wave is twice the distance between adjacent nodes
The wavelength equals the distance from a node to the nearest antinode
The wavelength is four times the distance between adjacent antinodes
questions.explanation: Nodes are evenly spaced points of zero displacement where the incident and reflected waves are opposite in phase and cancel; antinodes are points of maximum disturbance where the waves reinforce. The wavelength of the waves involved in the standing wave is twice the distance between adjacent nodes (or adjacent antinodes).

questions.q: A siren produces a sound of frequency 200 Hz that passes through a window. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m s⁻¹, calculate the wavelength of this sound to decide how much it will diffract.
working: This wavelength is large compared with the 35 cm window, so there is a large diffraction spread.
questions.explanation: Rearranging the wave equation v = fλ gives λ = 1.65 m (165 cm). Because the wavelength is large compared with the opening, the low-frequency sound diffracts strongly and spreads out, while a 10 000 Hz sound (λ ≈ 3.3 cm) barely diffracts.

questions.q: Water waves approach a boundary at which the wave speed changes from 40 cm s⁻¹ to 24 cm s⁻¹. If the waves initially had a wavelength of 10 cm, find their wavelength after they have crossed the boundary (refraction).
working: Frequency is unchanged at a boundary: \(f = \dfrac{v_1}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{40}{10} = 4\,\mathrm{Hz}\)
In the new medium the frequency stays 4 Hz, so \(\lambda_2 = \dfrac{v_2}{f}\)
questions.explanation: Refraction is a change in direction caused by a change in speed; the frequency stays constant (set by the source) while the wavelength tracks the new, slower speed. The waves slow down, so the wavelength gets shorter and the waves 'bunch up'.

questions.q: The amount of diffraction that occurs depends on the wavelength of the waves. When waves diffract through a gap of width w in a barrier, the ratio of wavelength to gap width is important — so what happens to the amount of diffraction as the wavelength gets longer, and when the wavelength is less than the size of the object?
options: The shorter the wavelength, the more diffraction occurs
The longer the wavelength, the more diffraction occurs; as the ratio λ/w increases, so does the amount of diffraction
Diffraction is the same for all wavelengths through a given gap
Diffraction only occurs when the wavelength is much smaller than the gap
questions.explanation: The amount of diffraction depends on the wavelength: the longer the wavelength, the more diffraction occurs. For a gap of width w, the ratio λ/w matters — as it increases, the amount of diffraction increases. This is why long-wavelength sound diffracts around a freeway barrier while short-wavelength sound leaves a shadow.

questions.q: From memory: state the condition for resonance and what happens to the amplitude when that condition is met.
keyPoints: Resonance occurs when an object is exposed to a driving frequency equal to the object's natural frequency.
This increases the amplitude of the object's vibration (energy is transferred efficiently each cycle, building the amplitude).
The driving frequency is the frequency of a forced vibration; the natural frequency is the rate inherent to the object's structure.
Examples: an opera singer shattering a wine glass, or pushing a child on a swing at its natural rhythm.
questions.explanation: The key relationship is driving frequency = natural frequency → maximum amplitude. The swing analogy captures it: small pushes timed to the natural rhythm build a large amplitude because energy accumulates each cycle.

questions.q: A tuning fork tuned to the A above middle C vibrates at 440 Hz whenever it is struck. What does this illustrate about natural vibration?
options: The frequency depends on how hard the fork is hit
The natural vibration is the rate at which the object oscillates once set in motion, inherent to its structure — determined by the metal, its length and the spacing of its prongs
The tuning fork only vibrates when driven by another vibrating object
The natural frequency changes each time the fork is struck
questions.explanation: Natural vibration is the rate at which an object oscillates once set into motion and is inherent to its structure. A struck tuning fork vibrates at the same rate regardless of how hard it is hit, because its rate is set by its material, length and prong spacing — here 440 Hz, its natural frequency.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a progressive (travelling) wave and a standing wave in terms of energy?
options: A progressive wave stores energy in fixed nodes; a standing wave carries energy from place to place
A progressive wave transports energy through the medium, while a standing wave does not transport energy along the medium — it stores energy in a fixed pattern of nodes and antinodes
Both transport energy at the same rate in opposite directions
Neither carries nor stores energy; they only transfer momentum
questions.explanation: A progressive wave moves energy from a source to somewhere else. A standing wave does not transport energy along the medium; the energy stays put, sloshing between the nodes, stored in the oscillation. If a question describes fixed points that never move and a pattern that doesn't travel, it's a standing wave storing energy.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of superposition, how a standing wave forms, and define a node and an antinode. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: A standing wave forms when two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions through the same medium — for example, an incident wave and its reflection — and superpose. By the principle of superposition their displacements add at every point. At points where the two waves are always out of phase, the displacements always cancel, producing nodes — points of permanently zero displacement. At points where the two waves are always in phase, the displacements always reinforce, producing antinodes — points of maximum oscillation. Because the nodes and antinodes stay in fixed positions, the pattern appears to stand still.

criteria.descriptor: Two identical waves (same frequency and amplitude) travelling in opposite directions superpose.
Appeals to the principle of superposition (displacements add at every point).
Out-of-phase cancellation gives nodes — points of zero displacement.
In-phase reinforcement gives antinodes — points of maximum displacement; pattern is fixed (standing).

questions.explanation: The weak answer is just 'the waves add up'. The marks are for naming the opposite-direction setup, the appeal to superposition, and the in-phase/out-of-phase conditions that produce fixed antinodes and nodes.
